summary: Learners enumerate every combination of two categories (e.g. 3 starters × 4 mains) systematically — holding the first choice fixed and running through every second choice before moving on — so that none is missed or repeated. Recording the combinations in a two-way grid or tree makes completeness arguable and reveals that the total equals the PRODUCT of the options in each category (3 × 4 = 12), not their sum (3 + 4 = 7). This is an early foundation of multiplicative counting for Year 6.
misconceptions: Lists haphazardly, so combinations are missed or duplicated and completeness cannot be judged
Cannot tell whether all the combinations have been found
Predicts the total by ADDING the options (3 + 4 = 7) instead of multiplying (3 × 4 = 12)
Changes both choices at once (e.g. only the diagonal S1M1, S2M2, S3M3), losing track of the rest
Believes there are only a handful, stopping before the set is complete

activities.title: Pair and light the grid: building every meal in order
steps: Start with 3 starters and 4 mains and first PREDICT how many different meals you think are possible before listing any — write down your prediction and say whether you think it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.

Begin by pairing starters and mains in any order you like, recording each meal you make in a two-way grid (starters down the side as rows, mains across the top as columns) by marking the matching cell.
Look at the grid: check whether random pairing has left scattered marked cells with empty gaps, or whether you tried to mark any meal twice. Ask yourself: have I found them all? Can I be sure?
Now switch to a fixed order: hold starter 1 and pair it with every main in turn (filling a whole ROW), then starter 2's row, then starter 3's row, until every cell is marked with no gaps.
Count the completed grid as rows × columns = 3 × 4 = 12, and compare this with your earlier prediction.
Explain how you know you have found every meal, and why the total is 3 × 4 rather than 3 + 4.
activities.insight: Working in a fixed order — fix one choice, run through every option of the other — guarantees no combination is missed or repeated, and the complete set fills a grid whose total is rows × columns, the product of the options.

activities.title: The tree-diagram route to the same complete set
steps: Draw a tree: one branch for each starter, then from each starter branch draw a sub-branch for every main.
Read each complete path from left to right as one meal (e.g. starter 1 → main 3).
Count the end-points of the tree and check it matches the grid total of 12.
Explain why each starter branch must sprout the same 4 sub-branches, so the total is 3 lots of 4 = 3 × 4.
activities.insight: A tree diagram is a second systematic structure that enumerates the same complete set; the repeated identical sub-branching is the product 3 × 4 made visible a different way.

activities.title: Check and extend: how many if a category grows?
steps: Answer 'How many meals are there altogether?' and justify whether it is 3 + 4 or 3 × 4.
Fill in a deliberately missing combination given a partly-completed grid or list.
Predict, WITHOUT listing them all, how many meals there would be if the café added a 4th starter (4 × 4 = 16), explaining your reasoning from the product structure.
Match each listed meal to its grid cell to confirm the set is complete and non-repeating.
activities.insight: The product structure lets you predict the count when a category grows without enumerating every case, confirming the skill transfers beyond the original numbers.

checkQuestion: A café offers 3 different starters and 4 different mains. List every possible meal of one starter and one main, and show me how you know you have listed them all. Then tell me how many meals there are altogether, and why.
checkAnswer: 12 meals — each of the 3 starters paired with each of the 4 mains (S1M1, S1M2, S1M3, S1M4, S2M1, …, S3M4), found by holding each starter and running through all four mains. The total is 3 × 4 = 12 (the product of the options), complete because every starter has been paired with every main.
